Enan
EE-nan
proper noun
Hebrew Enan (H5881), having eyes or fountain — from ayin (H5869), which in Hebrew is one word for both the eye and the spring of water.

Biblical Definition

Enan was a man of the tribe of Naphtali in the wilderness generation, named five times in Numbers and only ever as the father of Ahira, prince of Naphtali (Num 1:15; 2:29; 7:78, 83; 10:27). No act of his is recorded. The name rests on ayin, a word Hebrew uses for two things English keeps apart: the eye that sees and the spring that flows. The same noun stands in the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth (2Ch 16:9) and in the place-names of Israel's water — En-gedi, the spring of the kid; En-rogel; Enan itself. Both senses preach. A land that lives or dies by where the springs are learns to speak of God as a fountain: they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jer 2:13). And a people camped in a wilderness under the eye of God learns that being seen is mercy, not surveillance — Hagar, alone and cast out, named the God who found her Thou God seest me (Gen 16:13). Naphtali's captain was the son of a man called eyes, or spring, and both readings are true to the God of the wilderness.

Origin & Era

A man of Naphtali in the wilderness generation, father of Ahira prince of Naphtali; his name means eyes, or fountain.

ENAN, Hebrew Enan, having eyes, or fountain.

A man of the tribe of Naphtali in the generation that came out of Egypt.

Father of Ahira, prince and captain of the children of Naphtali.

Named five times in the book of Numbers, always as the father of Ahira.

From ayin, the Hebrew word for both an eye and a spring of water.

Key Scripture

Num 1:15 — "Of Naphtali; Ahira the son of Enan."

Num 2:29 — "Then the tribe of Naphtali: and the captain of the children of Naphtali shall be Ahira the son of Enan."

Num 7:78 — "On the twelfth day Ahira the son of Enan, prince of the children of Naphtali, offered:"

Num 10:27 — "And over the host of the tribe of the children of Naphtali was Ahira the son of Enan."

Modern Corruption

The all-seeing God is heard as a threat; Scripture offers His seeing first as the comfort of the afflicted.

expand to see more

An age trained to fear surveillance hears the doctrine of divine omniscience as the worst news of all — a watcher who misses nothing, keeping a record against us. Scripture knows that use of the truth and presses it on the impenitent: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13). But the first note the Bible strikes is the opposite one. The first person in Scripture to name God for His seeing is a runaway slave woman in a desert, pregnant, mistreated and utterly unrecorded by anyone else, and what she said was Thou God seest me (Gen 16:13). She meant it as rescue.

The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, and the verse says why: to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him (2Ch 16:9). Being seen by God is the ground of the afflicted believer's hope, because it means no wrong done to him in secret is unwitnessed and no faithfulness of his in obscurity is unrecorded. The principle to recover is that omniscience is a terror only to those who intend to go on sinning, and a consolation to everyone else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Enan (H5881), from ayin (H5869), an eye, and by the same word a spring or fountain of water.

expand to see more

Hebrew ayin (H5869) — an eye; also a fountain or spring, the two senses carried by one word.

Hebrew Enan (H5881) — the Naphtalite father of Ahira, Numbers 1:15, 2:29, 7:78, 7:83, 10:27.

Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a spring, a source; the fountain of living waters (Jer 2:13).

Hebrew roi (H7210) — seeing, a vision; Hagar's Thou God seest me, El-roi (Gen 16:13).

Greek pege (G4077) — a fountain, a spring; a well of water springing up into everlasting life (Joh 4:14).
